01

The short version

Open by refusing the singular. "<System> is not one system. It is N things that share <the thing they share>." Then one bullet per thing, each naming where it runs and what it owns. A reader who stops here should still be able to draw the boxes.

  • The first thing. Where it runs, what it owns, and the one fact about it that a reader would otherwise assume wrongly.
  • The second thing. Three to five bullets is the range. More than five means the decomposition is at the wrong altitude.
02

What the core is made of

  • One bullet per stage. Name the real component and its settings in monospace, then say in plain words what the setting buys.
  • Where a setting exists because something went wrong once, say so. That clause is usually the most credible sentence in the section.
03

One request, end to end

  1. The first hop. Name what goes out and what comes back, in the real field names. This list is the place for payload detail; the diagram stays coarse.
  2. The second hop. Where a value is deliberately narrowed, opaque, or withheld, say so and say why. That is a design decision, not an implementation detail.
  3. The end. Limits and ceilings belong here: timeouts, maximum durations, retry behaviour.
04

Everything that is not that path

The first loopA → B → C

A short paragraph per loop. Name the mechanism, the guarantee (signed, idempotent, versioned, gated) and the thing that makes it observable when it fails.

The loop that mattersA → B → C

Give the accent border to the loop that can change what the system does. Say plainly what stands between a change and production.

06

The seams

The sentence to open with: defects come from boundaries, not from the middle of components. Then the table. This is the most valuable section in the document, so write it last, when you know the system well enough to be precise about failure.

BoundaryWhat crossesHeld shut byWhen it fails
A → BThe actual payload, in field namesThe mechanism, not the intentionWhat the user or the operator sees
07

Decisions that put the lines where they are

  • State the decision, then its cost. A decision listed without its cost reads as a justification. "We chose X. The price is Y, and we have paid it N times" reads as engineering and is far more persuasive.
  • Include the uncomfortable one. Every system has a control that is weaker than a reader would assume. Naming it here, with its compensating control, is what makes the rest credible.
08

What is true today, and what is not

The stage it is at. Live, piloted, synthetic data, real data. Be exact.

What has not been measured. If the numbers start from zero, say they start from zero. Never round an unmeasured thing up to a claim.

What is half-finished. The unused component, the empty table, the migration applied on one side of a seam. A reader who finds one of these later discounts everything else.

What the vendor could change. Alpha features, deprecations, anything with a one-way door in it.
